name: Brown Green
lede: Brown Green is a very dark olive-grey, the name of a RAL factory paint colour, and in the books the same two words describe natural minerals, cotton and Chinese porcelain.

sections.title: A name from a paint chart
sections.body:
The swatch is #35382E, a dark neutral with a faint olive cast and lightness 23 [1]. Our library traces the name to RAL, the German colour standard first issued in 1927, where it is RAL 6008 [1]. The nearest named colour is [[gunmetal]], at a ΔE of 9.5 [1].

A second source gives a different colour under the same name: the xkcd survey of 2010 has brown green as #706C11, a far yellower olive [1]. The two lists do not agree, and the name is plain enough that both are reasonable. Close neighbours are [[olive]] and [[moss]] [1].

sections.title: Where brown-green turns up
sections.body:
The books use the words as a plain description of nature rather than as a colour with a history. The Pigment Compendium says the mineral augite ranges from brown-green through light and dark brown to black, that biotite mica is usually black but can be brown-green, and that pyrophyllite has brown-green varieties [2]. These are natural rocks whose colour varies with impurities [2].

In cotton, conventional breeding long gave only browns, greens, yellows and rusts, and the blues stayed elusive; in 1996 Calgene was granted the first US patent for transgenic colour alteration, aimed at black, red and blue cotton, in Balfour-Paul's account [3]. Finlay describes Chinese brown-green porcelain, the celadon, and a young museum worker who told her its appeal was its simplicity and its closeness to nature [4]. See [[celadon]] for the glaze itself.

The pair also matters for the eye. In deuteranopia, a form of red-green colour blindness, green can be seen as brown, and brown, green, yellow, orange and red are hard to tell apart [5]. Brown and green are also two of the eleven basic colour terms in Berlin and Kay's study of 98 languages [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This is a common painted colour. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 2,112 contain it, or 8.88 per cent, more common than 94 per cent of the named colours [7]. It peaks in the 1700s, in 7.9 per cent of 3,449 paintings, only 1.2 times the rate of the same museums as a whole [7]. Inside a painting it is most often a mid-tone, in 44 per cent of the 1,596 paintings that hold it by lightness rank [7].

The painters who lean on it hardest are [[painter:erik-pauelsen|Pauelsen]] (7 of 15 works), [[painter:pieter-van-der-werff|Pieter van der Werff]] (12 of 35) and [[painter:gustave-courbet|Courbet]] (10 of 50) [7]. It shares canvases with [[ebony]] and [[bronze-lustre]] more than chance [7]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a match is a screen colour, not a pigment test [7].

The oldest match, a 1099 Japanese sutra wrapper, is 828 years older than the name, so it is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a sign of any dye [7]. Look for it in the shadowed trees and dark earth of Dutch and Danish landscapes, where [[painting:nga-50602|a view of the Amazon shore]] by Catlin shows it as a shadow colour [7].
